title: Experimental forest gaps increase beetle diversity via abundance‐mediated effects
content:
In a full-factorial well-replicated forest gap experiment, we found that beetle diversity is higher in forest gaps than in closed forest via an abundance-mediated mechanism. Given that the frequency of natural disturbances is increasing, such understanding is becoming increasingly important for predicting biodiversity responses to environmental change.


Abstract

Forest gaps increase the heterogeneity and energy availability in a forest stand as they are accompanied by higher canopy openness and, under natural conditions, the occurrence of larger quantities of deadwood. Therefore, open-land and deadwood-dependent species may colonise gaps, potentially explaining the frequently reported higher local species diversity of gaps compared to closed forests. Higher energy availability in forest gaps could also increase species abundance, and subsequently diversity, via a ‘more individuals’ mechanism. However, to disentangle the responses of species diversity to forest gaps with and without deadwood enrichment, experimental approaches are needed. We sampled beetles, one of the most diverse taxa in forests, in a large-scale, full-factorial and well-replicated experiment at 26 sites in three regions of Germany (treatments: Control, Deadwood, Gap, Gap + Deadwood). We tested for changes in abundance, observed and standardised diversity, the community weighted means of body size and the share of forest and open-land specialist beetles in response to experimental gap creation and deadwood enrichment. Total beetle abundance and diversity were higher in gaps than in closed forests. However, in line with a ‘more individuals’ mechanism, the effect on diversity was mediated by increases in abundance. Once diversity was standardised by sample coverage, treatment effects on diversity vanished. We found that beetle communities in forest gaps consisted of on average larger species than in closed forests. The share of individuals from forest-specialist beetles was lower in the Gap than in the Deadwood and Gap + Deadwood treatments. However, the higher share of open-land specialist beetles in forest gaps compared to closed forests was negligible. We show that forest gaps are inhabited by larger-bodied and more diverse beetle communities, which could be due to enhanced resource availability and higher activity rates resulting from more favourable microclimatic conditions. A higher species abundance mediated the positive effect of forest gaps on beetle diversity. Our results furthermore highlight that disentangling responses of biodiversity to changing habitat conditions inherently depends on full-factorial experiments.
